travelAdvisory.summary:
Reissued after periodic review with minor edits.                 

Exercise normal precautions in Poland.
Read the country information page for additional information on travel to Poland.
If you decide to travel to Poland:                                  

Enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive messages and Alerts from the U.S. Embassy and make it easier to locate you in an emergency.
Review the Country Security Report for Poland.
Prepare a plan for emergency situatio

healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Poland. Emergency numbers (112/999/997/998), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, travel insurance advice, and vaccination recommendations.

connectivity.simOptions: Play, Orange, or T-Mobile prepaid SIMs at airport shops or any 'salon' in the city. Cheap data — 20GB for ~30-40 PLN. Need passport.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes, restaurants, hotels, and shopping malls. Quality is generally good. Many cities have free municipal WiFi.
connectivity.bestOption: Play prepaid SIM for best value and coverage. eSIM via Airalo or Holafly works well. EU roaming applies if you have an EU SIM.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants is customary. Round up for taxis. Not expected at bars for simple drinks. Say 'reszta dla pana/pani' (keep the change).
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in cities. Cover shoulders and knees in churches. Poland is quite fashionable — avoid looking too touristy.
cultural.greetings: Handshake with eye contact. Close friends kiss on both cheeks. Use Pan (Mr) / Pani (Mrs) until invited to use first names. Poles value politeness.
taboos: Confusing Poland with Russia or calling it Eastern Europe (it's Central Europe)
Making light of WWII or the Holocaust
Refusing food or drink when offered as a guest
Sitting at the corner of a table (superstition — won't marry for 7 years)
Giving even numbers of flowers (reserved for funerals)
cultural.haggling: Not practiced. Prices are fixed at shops, restaurants, and most markets.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen). UK, EU, Australia, Canada, Japan also visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: May-September (warm, long days). June-August peak season. December for Christmas markets. Avoid November (grey, cold).

stalenessWarnings.message: Some data in this profile may be outdated. Connect to the internet to refresh.

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 997)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (997) and ambulance (999) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
